# *Leops (Fleet) uploads* the signed rental agreement to the fleet profile, + *uploads driver consent forms* to each driver’s profile when they also sign the sub-lease agreement with driver

To determine the capacity of the batteries at 0.2C load until 34V I used the Electronic Load EL 9080-45 DT and Electronic Load EL 9080-45 T.

Before the test both of the batteries were fully charged. Tests started at 41.5V which is the max voltage in the SOC calculation.

The the test were done using the battery test static function.

For testing I took 2 batteries. The first battery was with the *highest capacity* and the other was with the *lowest capacity*.

The load test ended when the batteries reached 34V. The batteries were discharged with 0.2C, because that is the current what the manufacturer used to define the capacity of the battery.'

Test results: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/12d2LcOQSIebEGQlyoTqawIOxm9GK31OdG6TeXcDIUME/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/12d2LcOQSIebEGQlyoTqawIOxm9GK31OdG6TeXcDIUME/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link] 

||*Battery serial nr.*||*Capacity when discharging with 0.2C (Wh)*||*Capacity when discharging with 7.5A (Wh)*||*Difference (Wh)*||
|DLB2010110096|414,73|508,4|93,67|
|DLM1912230012|398,58|412,6|16,02|

h2. Conclusion

its hard to predict what is the average amount of capacity what we would lose if we would raise the minimum voltage of the SOC calculation to 34V, from this small variety of batteries.
On *“good”* batteries we would *lose at most around 100 Wh* and on *“bad”* batteries we would *lose at most about 20 Wh*.
It seem that the 34V for minimum voltage is suitable, this in theory would remove the problem where the older K1 batteries would shut off output at lower SOC when load is higher.

Merlin and NCAB are unable to manufacture either Type IVb or Type VIb in conjunction to each other. The common technology they both manufacture is Type VIIb. The initial price difference indication between Type VIb vias and Type VIIb vias offered by NCAB is around 13%. Taking Würth's pricing as a basis, the results are plotted in sheet 2 of this document.

At 40€ and 50€ IOT cost price points the failure percentage from using Type IVb required to justify the higher cost of Type VIIb vias is in the range of 0.35%(59pcs.)-0.49%(12pcs.) at 16800-2400 total production quantities, respectively.

The bare PCB production lead time is "slightly longer" in the prototyping  phase, but stays the same according to Paul Machin from Merlin.

*Privacy notice by Production team:*

[https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KgPUm1O-LadF_gFOOBxuDl1wtfCunfCIGTIe6tQ3ZnA/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KgPUm1O-LadF_gFOOBxuDl1wtfCunfCIGTIe6tQ3ZnA/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 

*Key Issues Identified:*

# *Unclear Legal Basis*
The notice references artistic and journalistic exemptions under Article 85 GDPR and the Latvian Personal Data Processing Law, but does not explain clearly to data subjects what legal basis is being relied upon for the filming. Consent is not mentioned at all, and if legitimate interest is used instead, this requires more context to be meaningful and transparent to riders.
# *Limited Description of Data Subject Rights*
The only right mentioned is the ability to express objections before publication. The notice omits basic GDPR rights such as access, erasure (where applicable), or the right to lodge a complaint with the DPA.
# *Vague Wording on Editorial Control*
The language used to describe how objections will be handled ("we will consider your input to the extent possible") is vague and could give the impression that objections may not be respected in practice. It lacks a clear commitment to act upon valid concerns, such as removing or anonymising individuals who do not wish to appear.
# *No Mention of Data Retention or Safeguards*
There is no information about how long footage will be stored or what measures are in place to secure the data. While exemptions apply for journalistic/artistic work, a brief mention of retention or safeguards would support transparency and trust.
# *No Clarification of the Controller Role or Contact Path*
While the production company is named, the notice does not explicitly state that Aivis/AC Production is the sole controller responsible for the filming. It also does not offer clear guidance on how riders should raise data protection concerns.

*Focus of the feedback given to business stakeholder:*

Given Bolt's role as a separate controller with no involvement in the filming itself, I chose not to comment on every GDPR issue in the production team's draft privacy notice. Instead, I focused on points that are most likely to impact Bolt, either because they affect how riders perceive our involvement, or because they increase the risk of misdirected complaints.

I suggested including:

* A clear statement that Aivis/AC Production is the sole controller for the filming
* Contact details where riders can raise privacy-related questions
* A short explanation of what riders can do if they do not want to appear in published content
* A clear outline of what happens if someone objects (such as removal or anonymisation)

The goal here was not to make the notice overly legalistic, but simply to ensure that responsibilities are clearly communicated to riders. This helps prevent confusion, protects Bolt’s position, and limits our exposure in case complaints arise.

*Preliminary Legal Assessment*

This is only a preliminary assessment based on the lease terms and the Bauaufsichtsbehörde order and §§536, 536a BGB. If we want to take legal action, we should instruct external real estate counsel for a final legal opinion and litigation strategy.

# *Rent Abatement*

* *Contract and Law*: Under German law (§ 536 BGB), if a leased property has a defect that substantially reduces its suitability for the agreed use, rent is automatically reduced in proportion to the loss of usability. Our lease specifies the agreed use as e-bike and e-scooter logistics, storage, maintenance and charging of lithium-ion batteries (§ 2.1). The Bauaufsicht’s order prohibited this use in its entirety. Clauses in § 15 of the lease requiring notice before withholding rent do not remove the statutory abatement right, they only set procedural conditions.
* *Interaction with our permit duty*: The lease (§ 2.4 and § 9.5) obliges Bolt to obtain and maintain all permits necessary for our business, including a Nutzungsänderung where applicable. If the prohibition had been caused primarily or solely by our failure to secure such a permit, the landlord could argue that the defect is attributable to our own sphere of responsibility. In that case, the abatement claim under § 536 BGB could be reduced or excluded. However, in this case the Bauaufsicht order places the key remedial obligations on the landlord, specifically the requirement to file a Bauantrag and Brandschutzkonzept and to address multiple building-level fire safety deficiencies. This strongly suggests that the primary cause lies in the LL’s responsibility, not in a missing permit from our side.
* *Conclusion*: The prohibition rendered the premises completely unusable for the agreed purpose from 26.03.2025 to lease end. Based on the current evidence, there is a strong legal basis for a full rent reduction to zero for this period. The only legal risk is that the landlord could achieve a partial reduction of this claim if they prove that a missing Nutzungsänderung materially contributed to the prohibition.

# *Damages*

* *Contract and Law*: Under § 536a BGB, Bolt can claim damages if the LL is responsible for a defect that reduces or eliminates the agreed use of the property. The lease reinforces this by making the LL responsible for adequate building and operational fire safety, including preparing and paying for any Brandschutzkonzept (§ 6). The Bauaufsicht’s order addresses the LL directly, requiring them to submit a Bauantrag and Brandschutzkonzept and to correct a list of fire safety deficiencies. These are obligations in the LL’s sphere and not in Bolt’s.
* *Interaction with our permit duty*: § 2.4 and § 9.5 make Bolt responsible for obtaining and maintaining any permits required for our operations, including a Nutzungsänderung. If the main reason for the prohibition were our failure to secure a required change-of-use permit, independent of the fire safety defects, a court could reduce or exclude our damages claim. However, the fact that the authority’s order explicitly obliges the LL to take remedial actions and file core compliance documents supports the view that the primary cause of the order was on the LL’s side. The permit issue could still be raised by the LL to argue contributory fault (Mitverschulden) under § 254 BGB, which would proportionally reduce our recoverable damages.
* *Conclusion*: Based on current evidence, there is a reasonable legal basis to claim recovery of consequential costs. The main litigation risk is a reduction of these amounts if the landlord can prove that a missing or delayed Nutzungsänderung in our responsibility was a significant contributing factor to the prohibition.

*Final Conclusion*

We appear to have several strong arguments on our side, particularly where the Bauaufsicht’s order links the prohibition to LLs fire safety and building compliance obligations. However, this should not be treated as a final conclusion of the situation. The LL may also have credible arguments, especially around our obligation to secure a Nutzungsänderung, which could reduce our claims if a court finds it materially contributed to the prohibition. If we decide to pursue legal action, we should reassess the situation comprehensively with external real estate counsel to evaluate all arguments, risks, and evidentiary requirements from both sides.

Reviewed setup and made comments. Overall, I don’t think it is fully ready and have made the following considerations:

* *Risk*: Does not achieve deemed supplier - Art28 requires the agent to act in its own name. Current setup under B4B terms state SPV _does_ _not_ act in its own name in any capacity. This is not only inaccurate but also makes single invoicing not possible and increases agent-to-merchant risk to RH vertical.
* *Risk*: There’s a contractual buy-in of the ride without a contractual resell; SPV steps into the shoes of Passenger for all intents and purposes. Thus, SPV _does_ act in its own name. However, it’s not possible to reclaim VAT on this input purchase under the current B4B terms. 
* *Recommendation*: update B4B terms to reflect the reality that SPV is a procurement agent acting in its own name but behalf of the B4B customer. This puts SPV squarely on the buy side of the transaction, reducing regulatory and employment reclassification risk, while enabling Art28 deemed supplier treatment for VAT purposes. 
* *Recommendation*: more accurate descriptions of how the technology IP is distributed in the B4B terms. The *Driver App* is being sold to drivers by *Bolt Ops* for a commission; the *Rider App* is being given to users (including B4B users) by *Bolt Ops* for free; and the *B4B* *dashboard services* are being sold by Bolt Ops to SPV and resold by SPV to B4B customers for 10% commission.

*10.1 Documentation that the tenderer is not subject to grounds for exclusion*
{color:#bf2600}The documentation must be submitted in the form of a certificate or equivalent document issued in accordance with national rules in the tenderer's home country{color}, cf. Section 153(1) of the Public Procurement Act. {color:#bf2600}If the country in question does not issue such documents{color}, or if they do not cover all relevant grounds for exclusion in Section 135(1) or (3) and Section 137(1)(2) or (7) of the Public Procurement Act, they may be replaced by a sworn statement. If oaths are not used in the country in question, a solemn declaration made before a competent judicial or administrative authority, a notary public or a competent professional organisation in the country where the tenderer is established may be used, cf. Section 153(2) of the Public Procurement Act.
{color:#bf2600}It must be documented that neither the tenderer nor any members of the tenderer's board of directors, executive board, and/or supervisory board, nor any other persons who may have the power to represent, control, or make decisions in the tenderer's board of directors, executive board, or supervisory board, are subject to any of the grounds for exclusion.{color}
The documentation must not have been issued more than six months prior to the deadline for submission of tenders.
For Danish tenderers, the documentation must be submitted in the form of a service certificate from the Danish Business Authority. The service certificate can be obtained via the following link:
[https://indberet.virk.dk/myndigheder/stat/ERST/Anmod_om_serviceattest|https://indberet.virk.dk/myndigheder/stat/ERST/Anmod_om_serviceattest|smart-link] 
The contracting authority notes that when requesting a service certificate, information must be obtained from the bankruptcy court, the police, ATP, and the tax authorities. The tenderer should be prepared in advance to upload declarations of consent from members of the tenderer's board of directors, executive board, and supervisory board to the Danish Business Authority in connection with obtaining the service certificate.
Foreign tenderers are referred to the documentation provided in e-Certis, which can be found via the following link:
[https://ec.europa.eu/tools/ecertis|https://ec.europa.eu/tools/ecertis]

h2. *_10.1 Dokumentation for, at Tilbudsgiver ikke er omfattet af grundlag for udelukkelse_*

Dokumentationen skal fremlægges i form af en attest eller tilsvarende dokument udstedt i henhold til nationale regler i Tilbudsgivers hjemland, jf. udbudslovens § 153, stk. 1. Udsteder det pågældende land ikke disse dokumenter, eller dækker disse ikke alle relevante udelukkelsesgrunde i udbudslovens § 135, stk. 1 eller 3, og § 137, stk. 1, nr. 2 eller 7, kan de erstattes af en erklæring under ed. Anvendes edsaflæggelse ikke i det pågældende land, kan der anvendes en erklæring på tro og love, der er afgivet for en kompetent retslig eller administrativ myndighed, for en notar eller for en kompetent faglig organisation i det land, hvor Tilbudsgiver er etableret, jf. udbudslovens § 153, stk. 2. 

Det skal dokumenteres, at såvel Tilbudsgiver som medlemmer af Tilbudsgivers bestyrelse, direktion og/eller tilsynsråd og eventuelle andre personer, der måtte have beføjelse til at repræsentere, kontrollere eller træffe beslutning i Tilbudsgivers bestyrelse, direktion eller tilsynsråd, ikke er omfattet af udelukkelsesgrundene.

Dokumentationen må ikke være udstedt tidligere end 6 måneder før tilbudsfristen 

For danske tilbudsgivere skal dokumentationen fremlægges i form af en serviceattest fra Erhvervsstyrelsen. Serviceattesten kan indhentes via følgende link: 

[https://indberet.virk.dk/myndigheder/stat/ERST/Anmod_om_serviceattest|https://indberet.virk.dk/myndigheder/stat/ERST/Anmod_om_serviceattest|smart-link] 

Ordregiver gør opmærksom på, at der ved anmodningen om serviceattest skal bedes om, at der indhentes oplysninger fra Skifteretten, Politiet, ATP og Skat. Tilbudsgiver bør på forhånd være forberedt på, at der skal uploades samtykkeerklæringer fra medlemmer af Tilbudsgivers bestyrelse, direktion og tilsynsråd til Erhvervsstyrelsen i forbindelse med indhentning af serviceattesten.

For udenlandske tilbudsgivere henvises til den dokumentation, der fremgår af e-Certis, der kan findes via følgende link:

[+https://ec.europa.eu/tools/ecertis+|https://ec.europa.eu/tools/ecertis]

Hello, [~accountid:5bc4571d505b7a135722281f].

Please see below my answers and comments to your recent questions:

*Request T-Y Parks SIA and the daughter’s companies (T-Y Parks - 01, 02, 03) to cover any fines that might be imposed on Bolt (unpaid rental fees for the past 3 months per vehicle - Guarantee to ABC Rent)*

The cooperation agreement between Bolt and T-Y Parks SIA does not include an indemnity clause or any express obligation for T-Y Parks SIA (or its affiliates) to cover fines or penalties incurred by Bolt. The only relevant contractual mechanism is a refund obligation by T-Y Parks SIA under specific circumstances, as outlined in the agreement. This refund obligation would not automatically extend to covering fines unless explicitly linked to the defined refund circumstances.

As regards the guarantee, if T-Y Parks SIA fails to meet its obligations to ABC Rents (non-payment of rental fees), Bolt may be held liable under the guarantee. However, this liability arises from Bolt’s independent commitment to ABC Rents and is not automatically recoverable from T-Y Parks SIA unless there is a contractual basis for doing so.

If the intention is to secure reimbursement or indemnification from T-Y Parks SIA (and/or its affiliates) for any amounts Bolt may need to pay under the guarantee, an amendment to the existing contract or a separate indemnity agreement would be necessary to establish a clear legal obligation.

*Impose obligations or penalties on the Fleet for the initial installment paid by us, which was not honored over the full 4-year agreement period (i.e., clawback)*

As mentioned above, under the current terms of the cooperation agreement, the primary liability that can be imposed on the Fleet (T-Y Parks SIA) is the obligation to refund certain payments made by Bolt. This refund obligation is primarily linked to the Fleet’s non-performance of specific KPIs agreed upon in the contract. Thus the possibilities for a refund in this particular situation should be further explored based on the actual performance of the agreement by the Fleet.

*Our reach to recover any outstanding costs from other fleets that the Fleet Owner may own or be associated with?*

Unless there are explicit provisions in the cooperation agreement that extend liability to other entities owned or controlled by the Fleet Owner (e.g., group liability, joint and several liability clauses, or cross-default provisions), we cannot legally enforce recovery from those entities based solely on their association. If the associated fleets operate as separate legal entities (e.g., T-Y Parks – 01, 02, 03), they are treated as independent under the law, even if they are ultimately owned by the same individual or parent company. Without specific agreements in place, liability cannot be transferred or extended to them. Given this, we shall consider the option to amend the existing cooperation agreement or sign a specific one.

h3. *Top 10 Countries for Compliance Focus*

*Disclaimer:* This priority list is a synthesis of two key sources: the quantitative *Risk Scoring Model* (balancing GMV and systemic risk) and the qualitative insights from the [+*Rides Compliance Monthly Review (July 2025)*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vO10EQNilixXDdvOAFjiKLVzS8-a-IfqtUgFHo9uDUc/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.43xhas2uxpc5][+,+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vO10EQNilixXDdvOAFjiKLVzS8-a-IfqtUgFHo9uDUc/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.43xhas2uxpc5] which provides essential context on urgent, active government demands and ongoing projects.

* *Germany (Score: 20)*
** A Top 10 GMV market with "Significant" Regulatory Risk, driven by its highly restrictive Passenger Transport Act, which creates a challenging environment for ride-hailing models.
* *United Kingdom (Score: 20)*
** A Top 5 GMV market with "Significant" Regulatory Risk, stemming from the Supreme Court ruling that classified drivers as "workers", fundamentally challenging the self-employed model.
* *France (Score: 18)*
** As the #1 GMV Market, protecting its revenue is critical. The "High" regulatory risk reflects its complex labour laws and strong municipal oversight.
* *Spain (Score: 18)*
** A Top 15 GMV market with "Significant" regulatory risk, driven by specific labour laws and active government demands.
* *Netherlands (Score: 18)*
** A Top 25 GMV market with "Significant" regulatory risk, based on the influential 2021 Amsterdam Court of Appeal ruling that classified drivers as employees, creating a major systemic threat to the business model.
* *Portugal (Score: 18)*
** A Top 10 GMV market with "High" regulatory risk and a history of emerging labour law challenges. It is a country where the government is actively demanding supply documentation validation.
* *Thailand (Score: 16)*
** As the #2 GMV market, its "Moderate" risk is elevated by a known pattern of demanding localised solutions, such as the major ongoing insurance project.
* *Poland (Score: 16)*
** A Top 3 GMV market. Its priority is driven by active government demands for database validation, requiring immediate focus.
* *Romania (Score: 16)*
** A Top 10 GMV market. The priority is heightened by active government demands for automatic tax reporting to combat evasion.
* *South Africa (Score: 16)*
** A Top 5 GMV market with "Moderate" regulatory risk and ongoing debate around the national land transport act, making it a key market to protect.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancel it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance to compensate for the debt in their account?

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

*Clarification notes.*

Here is where snapshot file gets deleted: [https://github.com/jestjs/jest/blob/fe7f28c9d1941f5c2726831cd9d9e479b401610e/packages/jest-snapshot/src/index.ts#L143|https://github.com/jestjs/jest/blob/fe7f28c9d1941f5c2726831cd9d9e479b401610e/packages/jest-snapshot/src/index.ts#L143|smart-link] 

Jest deletes unmatched snapshots by default. Unmatched snapshot - is the snapshot for which we do not have a corresponding test.

The only way to skip deletion is to specify ignore regex:

{noformat}    // ignore snapshots of ignored tests
    if (testIgnorePatternsRegex && testIgnorePatternsRegex.test(testPath)) {
      return false;
    }{noformat}



For example, to ignore spec tests while executing comp tests we can use this amendment to {{jest.config.js}}:

{noformat}const testPathIgnorePatterns = config.runtimeExtension === ".js" ? [] : ["<rootDir>/" + config.sourceFolder + "/.*\\.js"];
+ testPathIgnorePatterns.push("<rootDir>/.*/test/spec/.*");{noformat}

With this change, jest will NOT delete any snapshot file in spec test.



But in this case, jest will still delete *unmatched snapshot in a comp tests*. For example, I created two unmatched snapshots in some other comp tests, and they got deleted by jest:

{noformat}Snapshot Summary
 › 2 snapshot files removed from 2 test suites.
   ↳   • src/platform/commerce/billing_report/test/comp/controllers/__snapshots__/SpainReport-spec.ts.snap
       • src/platform/commerce/billing_report/test/comp/controllers/__snapshots__/MonthlySummaryReport-spec.ts.snap

Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       4 passed, 4 total
Snapshots:   2 files removed, 0 total
Time:        10.096 s, estimated 12 s
Ran all test suites matching /src\/platform\/campaign\/subscription_benefits\/test\/comp\/get-cancelled-ride-upsell-modal-comp.ts/i.{noformat}



So, this is a *feature* of jest to delete unmatched snapshots by default even though they do not belong to the test suite which is currently getting executed.

Can we mitigate it still somehow? Yes. We can do something like

* run {{jest}}
* after that, check whether there are modified snapshots *outside* of the specified test directory / suite / etc.
** if there are => rollback those changes ({{git reset}})

Do we need to do that? I would rather no do that, it is too complex.

Instead, I would propose either

* reject this ticket
* or do the following:
when Jenkins runs tests, we do it with {{--ci}} flag. With this flag, jest *does not* updates snapshots. If there are unmatched snapshots, jest will not delete them but log it:

{noformat}yarn ctest --ci src/platform/campaign/subscription_benefits/test/comp/get-cancelled-ride-upsell-modal-comp.ts
<...>
All tests passed


Snapshot Summary
 › 2 snapshot files obsolete from 2 test suites. To remove them all, run `yarn run ctest -u`.
   ↳   • src/platform/commerce/billing_report/test/comp/controllers/__snapshots__/MonthlySummaryReport-spec.ts.snap
       • src/platform/commerce/billing_report/test/comp/controllers/__snapshots__/SpainReport-spec.ts.snap

Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       4 passed, 4 total
Snapshots:   2 files obsolete, 0 total
Time:        9.097 s, estimated 11 s{noformat}

We can grep these lines, and if there are lines like {{.*snapshot files obsolete.*}} → then we fail the CI. In particular, the check should be done on {{stdout}} of this line:

{noformat}Jenkinsfile:1108
runAndLog("yarn jenkins:run-on-server 'cd /server && date && ${tracingFlag} PARALLEL_TEST_RUNNER_SPLIT_NAME_AND_BATCH=${splitNameAndBatch} yarn ${type}test:ci --logHeapUsage'", "${logDir}/${logFile}");{noformat}

With that, instead of “reverting jest changes outside of the intended test suite”, we can fail CI “if there are unmatched snapshots detected”.

Firstly, we would need to delete all unmatched snapshots, and then deploy this check.

In general, I do not see a legal issue with using service categories (such as Comfort, Premium, etc.) based on transparent, objective, and agreed criteria. This allows customers to choose a service level that best fits their preferences  and needs.

However, I would raise a concern regarding any limitation that would exclude certain drivers from receiving airport orders solely because they do not meet the criteria for a specific category. Such filtering could significantly affect the income potential of the excluded drivers, as airport trips are typically among the most profitable.

In Sweden, as in other EU countries, there is a growing regulatory scrutiny over the classification of platform workers. Measures that appear to unilaterally restrict access to high-value business opportunities especially without transparent justification or the ability to appeal could be interpreted as exerting a level of control or direction typically associated with an employer and employee relationship.

Therefore, in my point of view, while service segmentation is generally a permissible solution, completely restricting certain drivers from accessing airport orders, if not carefully implemented and justified, could be seen as: (a) disproportionate limitation on business activity opportunities; (b) an indicator of employer-like control; and (c) a potential breach of equal treatment principles if not handled transparently and fairly.

If you intend to apply filters for airport rides (e.g., minimum rating or vehicle age), its is recommended to consider implementing them in a non-exclusive way, e.g., allowing access to airport rides for other categories but, if technically possible, prioritizing Comfort or Premium for customer matching. 

However, if you decide to proceed further with this initiative, it is recommended to ensure that a clear communication with drivers is in place as it may help mitigate legal and reputational risks, especially in light of the ongoing platform work regulation discussions in Sweden and across the EU.

Hope it helps, but please let me know if you have any questions or further legal help is needed. Thank you! 🙏

[~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] DeepL translation of the response:
In response to your email, we would like to explain that, in accordance with Article 10 of the Data Regulation, personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences shall be processed only by official authorities under the control of the law or when authorised by Union or Member State law providing for appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of data subjects. This means that personal data on criminal convictions and offenses may only be processed in cases specified by law and to the extent specified by law.
The Inspectorate draws attention to the fact that the information contained in the Criminal Register is restricted access information. The first part of Article 19 of the Criminal Records Act specifies the persons who have the right to request and receive information from the Criminal Records Register, including the following rights for employers under point 5 of the first part of that article - to request information necessary to verify the compliance of a natural person with the restrictions laid down in regulatory enactments when hiring them for employment or service (indicating the regulatory enactment that provides for the relevant restrictions). Thus, the law restricts the circle of persons who may access this register.
In view of the above, an employer has the right to request information from the Criminal Register about the criminal record of a specific person only if the regulatory enactments governing the specific sector prohibit the employment of a person with a criminal record in an employment relationship. In this case, these are objective circumstances that are of significant importance. By not obtaining information about a person's criminal record from the Criminal Register, the employer would be in breach of the law. On the other hand, such objective circumstances do not exist in cases where regulatory enactments do not prohibit a convicted person from holding a specific position.

In the opinion of the Inspectorate, it is not justified to request information about an employee's criminal record in cases where the regulatory act does not stipulate that employees with a criminal record may not hold the position in question.

We thank you for your follow-up and for the opportunity to clarify how the Bolt Assist category currently operates. Bolt recognizes and fully respects the rights of persons with disability as enshrined in the Equal Opportunities (Persons with Disability) Act (Cap. 413) and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to which Malta is a signatory.

We wish to address the specific points raised:

# *Service Hours*
The current service hours for Bolt Assist (05:00–00:00) reflect the limited pool of licensed wheelchair-accessible vehicles and trained drivers available in Malta. At present, we have three such vehicles in operation. Extending the service to 24/7 availability is unfortunately not feasible without additional licensed vehicles and drivers. We emphasise that this limitation does not arise from a company policy decision but from existing *structural constraints in the market*. As more vehicles are licensed and drivers are available, we remain committed to expanding both the service hours and availability.
# *Geographical Coverage*
Similarly, at present the Bolt Assist service is only available in Malta. This is again due to the very limited number of licensed accessible vehicles, none of which are currently based in Gozo. Bolt is open to working with Transport Malta and the CRPD to encourage and support the licensing of accessible vehicles in Gozo, with the aim of extending coverage in the future.
# *Vehicle Licensing and Approval*
We confirm that the three vehicles currently operating under the Bolt Assist category are licensed and approved as wheelchair-accessible vehicles by *Transport Malta* in accordance with *S.L. 499.68 (Light Passenger Services and Vehicle Hire Services Regulations)*. {color:#ff5630}Provide with the documentation?{color}



We emphasise that the regular ride-hailing services are assessable for everyone at any given hour. This specific category was implemented by Bolt to provide an *additional means* of transport for those with special needs.

Please note that Bolt remains committed to ensuring equality of access and inclusion for persons with disabilities. While this specific category is constrained by the limited number of licensed accessible vehicles available nationwide, we are actively exploring opportunities to expand the service, and we are fully prepared to collaborate with the CRPD and Transport Malta in identifying solutions to increase accessibility for users.

We appreciate your guidance in this matter and remain at your disposal for a further meeting or discussion to explore practical steps that could be taken collectively to improve availability of accessible vehicles in Malta and Gozo.

Hello everyone.

Regarding this, TVDE Law establishes a requirement for suitability in article 10.º, n.º, c) and article 11.º. Suitability for the activity of TVDE Driver entails not having convictions for sexual crimes.

The requirement for suitability is evaluated by the IMT, when determining the attribution of the TVDE Driver Certificate to a Driver. Non fulfillment of this requirement is reason for not attribution or revocation of the certificate by IMT.

However, article 14.º of TVDE Law clearly states that:

_1 - The electronic platform operator is obliged to ensure full and permanent compliance with the requirements for the exercise of the activity provided for in this law, including those relating to vehicles and TVDE service operators._
_2 -_ *_The electronic platform operator must block access to the services provided by the platform by TVDE operators, drivers, or vehicles that do not comply with any of the requirements referred to in this law, whenever it has or should have knowledge of such non-compliance_*_._
_3 -_ *_Access to the electronic platform by TVDE drivers who do not meet the requirements referred to in the previous paragraph or who have ceased to meet them after accessing the activity is the responsibility of the respective operator_*_, without prejudice to the powers conferred on the IMT, I. P., and other supervisory bodies._

Therefore, +we have legal basis to block this driver, although I would recommend we inform the IMT, so that they, as the supervisory entity, can proceed to revoke this driver’s TVDE Certificate, or other measures deemed appropriate+.

Hi [~accountid:6352bddb13f37118d7258a9a] , see my comments below 🙂 

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
h3. _When no unsubscribe link is needed_
{panel}

If the SMS is purely transactional or service-related, you are not required to include an unsubscribe mechanism. This covers messages such as:

* Trip-related alerts (e.g., fiscalization issues, payouts, verification status)
* Service interruptions or updates that affect how the app or platform functions
* Regulatory compliance notifications

These are not considered direct marketing under Polish law or GDPR, and opt-outs do not apply.

:done: The message about trip non-fiscalization _did not require_ the “To unsubscribe” link. Removing it in the future for similar cases is both compliant and preferable to reduce confusion.

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
h3. When the unsubscribe is mandatory
{panel}

If the SMS promotes or nudges toward any *commercial gain* for Bolt, such as:

* Encouraging more rides or shifts
* Advertising new driver bonuses, promo periods, new service lines
* Referrals, upgrades, or optional features (like Bolt Drive)

--> then it counts as direct marketing, and under Polish rules (B2C: opt-in), an opt-out link is mandatory.

🔴 *Poland is a high-risk jurisdiction* for privacy enforcement on direct marketing, so we must stay strict here.

We are waiting for a decision from the Polish privacy regulator regarding direct marketing investigation, and we expect them to be strict.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. Some options to reduce friction
{panel}

# *For transactional SMS* - remove the unsubscribe text entirely, no legal need, and this avoids triggering scam concerns. This frees up character space too.
# *For marketing SMS*:
#* Use URL shorteners or redirects to save space 
#* Consider non-SMS formats like push notifications for marketing
#* Segment by consent status to limit sends only to those opted in (if not already in place)
# *To reduce scam risk on marketing SMS*:
#* Avoid generic phrasing like “Click here”
#* Add identifiers like “Bolt PL:” at the start of the SMS to increase legitimacy
#* Optionally, include SMS sender name as "BoltPL" if supported by the provider

The DESC Regulations were [analysed|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07T6MZ1USU/p1748874891294849?thread_ts=1748846834.428809&cid=C07T6MZ1USU] in June 2025 from a Privacy perspective, specifically in relation to their potential data localization requirements.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Findings*

* The Regulation introduces a data localisation requirement — but it *only applies to* _“_*_classified data_*_”_, which is defined as "_non-public information explicitly designated as sensitive or confidential_ {{by the government entity itself}}".
* *The classification decision therefore rests with DTC*. That gives us some strategic room to work: not all user or operational data will necessarily be considered “classified”.  However, we need to keep in mind that the DESC can audit DTC, as a Government entity in Dubai.
* *No blanket restriction on accessing data from outside the UAE* — remote access (e.g. by HQ teams in Estonia) is not prohibited in these Regulations, provided adequate security and access controls are in place
* *No requirement to store all data in the UAE* — only data classified as “classified” needs to be localised. Everything else can remain in our existing infrastructure

*Next steps*

* We should engage with DTC to help them make those distinctions (between _Classified_ and _Non-Classified_ data) clearly and proportionately. DTC will likely get its own legal interpretation done.
* From my review of this specific Regulation, the localisation requirement is a manageable and contained requirement, assuming DTC doesn’t apply an overly broad classification.
* I believe AWS has a Region in the UAE, which we could leverage for any data that DTC does choose to classify as 'Classified'.
{panel}

I separately analysed them again as part of the [RTA Security Audit|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-54576], my findings and suggestions were as follows:

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
* *The DESC's Information Security Regulations (ISR)*
* As I mentioned initially, my biggest concern about this exercise has been the potential for RTA to decide that based on our classifications, we must store data locally in Dubai — enforce a hard data localization requirement.
* In the ISR, all '{{Critical/Classified Data}}' must be stored locally - *Sub Control – 13.2.1*, _IF_ designated as such by a Government Entity or a Critical Non-government Entity (CNE).
* {{Critical/Classified Data}} is defined as including: 'Confidential', 'Sensitive' and 'Secret' — which RTA uses in it's Classification Guideline and which we've applied.
* From further reading in RTA's [+Cloud Security Assessment template+|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1M5SgAyXn-_564QpCSDKQh4nO3dx79rHrHirpKEYci_0/edit?gid=201731418#gid=201731418&range=C29], I can see that they have quoted word for word obligations from the ISR. The most important one relates to data localization, which means RTA clearly views the ISR as being applicable: {{Information Processing Location}}: "_Prevents handling and storing classified data with a Cloud Service Provider (CSP), outside the legal jurisdiction or geographical boundaries of the United Arab Emirates, including for CSP’s Backup or Disaster Recovery purposes_".
* *Do the ISRs apply to Bolt/DTC?*
** Initially I was under the impression that DTC would be subject to the ISR as DTC it is partially government-owned. However, I have done further analysis and I no longer consider the ISR applicable to Bolt, or DTC for that matter.
** Bolt and DTC, are not “_Dubai Government Entities_” as defined under the [+Dubai Electronic Security Centre Law – Law No. 15 of 2024+|https://dlp.dubai.gov.ae/Legislation%20Reference/2024/Law%20No.%20%2815%29%20of%202024%20Concerning%20the%20Dubai%20Electronic%20Security%20Centre.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com] (Art 2).
** DTC is a government-owned public joint stock company and, under the DESC law, such “government companies” are treated as *non-government entities* unless formally designated by DESC as a *Critical Non-government Entity (CNE) —* as far as I'm aware, DTC has not been designated a CNE, but we need to confirm with DTC
* 
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*We are meeting with DTC to get their opinion on my analysis and to conclude whether DTC is a CNE. If not, we will push for a conclusion that the ISRs are not applicable to DTC or Bolt and this ticket can be closed.*
{panel}

I think the preferred criteria are highlighted in the PP documents:

# [Strategy|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bw3jEbQxgbsqp7KXabr7sBc8W5tO0HvOr6iPEfSkCAk/edit?tab=t.0] - section titled “Example of what criteria we can ‘live with’ vs. not”
# More detailed PP “[waterfall|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vpKWdTSlgfPD-G46_BYn1ifsfbVQiH1SogbM8DJ1WNc/edit?tab=t.0]” - section 3 “criteria” sets out a list of “Criteria we likely don’t trigger” 

Both of these criteria are substantially based on the YODEL criteria (analysed in the [PWD legal analysis|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ChFdflsFqe2ZuOGr2NHoC5Z9I3Yy9sUdgprRVJabr5o/edit?tab=t.0] for more context), with some tweaks to make them more favourable to us.  I understand that the criteria highlighted in the documents above might not be in an ideal “copy-and-paste” format that we could send to legislators that they could use “as is”. But I would assume that the final wording is up to them and we should provide them with a short, to-the-point list of criteria we would like to see.

We discussed it again and looked into specific PWD workgroup documents across member states. Based on these, we still think that a “one-size fits all” wording probably isn’t feasible. Couple of examples to illustrate:

# *Form of transposition:* It’s not clear whether PWD transposition will be done through _new standalone laws_ or by _amending existing ones_. For example, the seven clauses in the L[T transposition document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XS0oSgX-f2zExP-ICJPZAkd7s6qCOtsK/edit] are very country-specific (drafted as amendments to existing law) and wouldn’t translate across borders.
# *Substantive differences in clauses:* Clauses will not be implemented in the same way. As an example, if we compare the fleet–platform joint liability clause:
## In [*Poland*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nHdFSieiPrWHc-SGXtLZIhswb0tNC8J-/edit], policymakers are pushing for _fleet-only liability_ (no joint liability) - while this is unlikely to happen, the starting point is quite different.
## In [*Croatia*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/15u_U_qXG6OA67y4NJgw_7VkU3jJO-bbd/edit], platforms may be exempt from joint liability under certain conditions.
## In [*Lithuania*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XS0oSgX-f2zExP-ICJPZAkd7s6qCOtsK/edit], the current draft wording seems to be harsher towards platforms than the PL and HR starting positions.

Based on that, we still think the approach of having a global unified strategy with specific main “goals” makes more sense. Lobbying is more that just legal drafting - so the legal team should make sure that the public policy team has a [clear understanding of the legal framework|https://docs.google.com/document/d/15zazIHfZcbhwjEeVPJemL4lAGLKdAqbycoZYIAA7wd4/edit?tab=t.0], so their positions based on the unified strategy are grounded in reality and are legally correct.

Hi [~accountid:712020:16feeee2-7721-43a0-8e2d-529b2d00b3e8], thank you for reaching out to us. 

Please find below legal advice related to this matter:

*Nature of Bolt’s Service*

* Bolt Operations OÜ provides an *information society service* (digital intermediary).
* Bolt does not provide transport services and does not employ drivers. Transport is carried out by independent Transportation Service Providers or their authorised persons.
* *Contractual Relationship*
** The relationship with drivers is governed by the General Terms for Drivers.
** The Terms specify:
*** Ride fares and distance are calculated by GPS-based systems and algorithms (Art. 4.6, 4.7).
*** Declining rides within the set radius affects the acceptance rate and account availability.
*** Bolt may suspend or block accounts in case of repeated violations (Art. 4.18, 4.19).
*** No employment relationship is created between Bolt and drivers (Art. 10.2, 10.3).
* *Allegations of “Mobbing” or Workers’ Rights Violations*
** These are legally misapplied since Bolt is not the employer.
** Drivers are independent contractors engaged via fleet operators or as sole traders.
* *Threats of Lawsuit Against Bolt’s Director*
** Any legal action must be directed against Bolt Operations OÜ, a legal entity incorporated in Estonia, not against individual directors.
** Directors cannot be held personally liable for contractual matters with Bolt.

PayU last reply was referring to the idempotency feature for cancel/capture explained in the email thread (Failed payments (PMOPS-8): 
We have investigated this matter and confirmed that the PayU South Africa platform did not respond in time to the Capture or Void requests initially initiated by Bolt, which resulted in a timeout.

Due to the lack of a timely response, the PayU Hub platform returned a 503 response code error, and as a result, no transaction resources were created on PayU Hub. Although the payment provider did not respond within the expected timeframe, these requests were successfully processed by the PayU South Africa platform.

Since the initial Capture or Void requests were completed successfully on the PayU South Africa side, any subsequent Create Capture or Create Void requests sent to the payment provider failed, as the payments were already marked as Captured or Voided in their system at that point.

To overcome [500]/[503] HTTP responses and safely retry requests, we strongly recommend implementing the [idempotency feature|https://developers.paymentsos.com/docs/apis/payments/1.3.0/#section/Overview/Idempotency].

The PayU HUB offers the idempotency feature, which allows a safe retry window. First, the merchant needs to include an idempotency header with each request. Its value needs to be unique. If one of the specific HTTP responses above were received for a transaction, the merchant could retry this transaction using the same idempotency header used in the original failed transaction. The PayU HUB then will first check if it has this request existing in the system. If not, it'll query the payment provider for the transaction details and status. If the provider has received it, the system will create a resource for it.

The idempotent safe window is 24 hours, meaning that the merchant has 24 hours to retry any transactions that have failed with 500 or 503 HTTPS responses. Otherwise, no action will be made, and these payments will not have Authorization/Charge/Void/Refund transaction resources.

It is essential to note that the merchant is responsible for handling these cases and retrying transactions with the same idempotency only when the situation requires it.

The idempotency feature should not be used to retry any other failed transactions, as it can cause transaction and processing issues.

Hi [~accountid:712020:eb9cd4dd-46ca-47c8-a985-9f940495724a], thanks for raising these points – let me clarify.



* *Role of Corezoid*: From my understanding, Bond is not looking to fully assign the API integration to Corezoid. Instead, Corezoid would act purely as an aggregator between Bolt API and Bond API endpoints, similar to how it works with Sryve.

BR,

* How much the reclassification risk increases if we are principal in food delivery?
** If we adopted the RO model (i.e. Bolt would be principal only for tax and invoicing purposes, but would not be liable for the delivery), then the reclassification risk would not increase significantly. 
** If we adopted a full principal model (i.e. Bolt would be the party to the delivery agreement and ultimately liable for carrying out the delivery and the quality of the delivery), this would increase the reclassification risk significantly more than the RO model, since we would explicitly state in our TCs that we are a party to the delivery agreement. 
** However, in both of these cases, ultimately substance over form matters in reclassification cases. Therefore, the courts are likely to take into account the actual day-to-day control that Bolt exercises over couriers (e.g. blocking due to AR, performance standards), regardless of the operating model. 
* In RO what is the change in the reclass risk assessment after localization and principal in substance? 
** Under our TCs, Bolt is the principal only for tax and invoicing purposes.Bolt is not a party to the delivery agreement and would not be liable for the delivery under the TCs.  Therefore, the reclassification risk did not increase significantly. 
* If we are principal only for the delivery part (not food part), would it also require changing the contracts with restaurants? 
** No, Bolt does not need to act as a principal for restaurant contracts. There might be some minor amendments needed to the restaurant contracts due to some references to the courier TCs, however Bolt does not need to act as a principal in relation to the the restaurants / food sales.  
* Could we be principal *without localization* from a legal perspective? 
** Yes, localisation and the principal model are two different topics from the legal side and Bolt can become principal without localisation. However, due to tax considerations (as explained above), it makes sense to localise the business along with the changes to the principal model. 

*Context on Localised Structure and Tax Model Alignment*

The idea of transitioning other markets to a localised structure has come up in other discussions—primarily as a strategy to manage the same tax risks we faced in Romania (RO). Therefore, this current proposal appears to be aligned with that broader approach.



*Key Distinction in the RO/BG Model*

In Romania and Bulgaria (RO/BG), we adopted a “reseller/principal” model solely for tax purposes. Practically, this means that:

* Bolt submits invoices in its own name, but on behalf of the Courier.
* For VAT purposes, Bolt acts as a “tax commissioner.”



However, from a legal and contractual standpoint (under our Terms & Conditions):

* Bolt is not a reseller or principal.
* We do not assume legal liability for delivery services. The Courier remains the direct contractual party to the customer and responsible for delivery quality, while Bolt handles refunds in practice

This approach helps us manage tax exposure without increasing our legal exposure. But we must also note that:

* In practice, Bolt does compensate customers for poor delivery experiences.
* This leads to the argument of "substance over form", as raised by EY.



Despite what we claim in our T&Cs, EY considers Bolt to be the principal based on actual business conduct.

*From legal perspective:*

* substance over form will likely prevail.
* That said, we should avoid giving regulators extra arguments by *explicitly stating in our T&Cs* that Bolt is the contracting party for delivery services.
** Such a statement would directly suggest *control over delivery quality*—a strong point in reclassification cases.
* However, if we’re *required to disclose* this in the Annual Report, we may not be able to fully avoid that risk.
* Regarding IPO readiness:

* *Some level of misalignment* between legal documents (T&Cs) and business operations may be unavoidable.

Deployment of Elastic KSPM is essentially DaemonSet-based deployment of Elastic Agent. DaemonSet means a running Docker container on each node of the cluster. 

The DaemonSet runs Elastic Agent with Kibana Fleet system. The container runs in privileged mode. It mounts /etc, /var etc into the container. Therefore the same DaemonSet can be used for other security monitoring purposes.

The only integration policy that will be loaded onto the Elastic Agent is the “unmanaged” KSPM integration policy. We will not currently enable the System or Metrics integrations because it is not necessary.

Difference between Elastic Agent “unmanaged” and “EKS” policies is that the “EKS” variant uses AWS APIs to pull some data from AWS. For that, it needs an IAM role or access keys.

Hi [~accountid:712020:cb7d1436-9800-43db-821c-db7028a6ff03] !

Under Subsidiary Legislation 499.68 (Light Passenger Transport Services and Vehicle Hire Services Regulations), every operator of light passenger service vehicles (including RH fleets) must have access to a garage or depot that complies with planning and regulatory standards.

This garage requirement ensures that operators have facilities to safely park and maintain their fleet.

Typically, the garage must be licensed or approved by Transport Malta (TM) and must also hold the relevant Planning Authority (PA) permit for change of use to “vehicle depot/garage.”

Bolt is not directly responsible for ensuring that a fleet’s garage has the correct planning permit. The responsibility lies with the fleet operator as the licensed entity.

Bolt’s responsibility is ensuring that all fleets/operators on the platform hold a valid operator license. On other hand, Bolt is not responsible for ongoing monitoring of whether the operator is in breach of every single operational condition (garage permits, tax compliance, etc.). That responsibility is on the operator, and TM is the enforcement authority.

Therefore, *can you please confirm that WT Global has a valid operator license and when was the last time that that Fleet provided us with information regarding their license?* 

According to SL 499.68, whenever an Operator asks for the renewal of their license, they have do provide all the information regarding the garage(s) being used. Therefore, if we are sure that their license was renewed and is valid, Bolt is compliant and does not have obligation to take any measure.

Thank you!

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Situation summary*
{panel}

* Bolt intends to notify UK drivers about a webinar hosted by Matrix IQ.
* Matrix IQ will promote their own CCTV hardware and explain council compliance issues.
* The purpose of the webinar is to generate product sales.
* Communication will be sent via in-app push and in-app inbox messaging.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Key issues and assessment*
{panel}

* The content is commercial in nature and intended to promote a third party's products.
* Even though Bolt does not transfer driver personal data, the act of distributing the promotion on behalf of Matrix IQ constitutes third-party marketing.
* Under UK PECR and GDPR, third-party marketing requires prior opt-in consent.
* In-app push and inbox messages fall within the scope of direct marketing when they:
** Are targeted based on user data, and
** Promote a commercial offer not provided by Bolt.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*Recommended actions*
{panel}

* Target only drivers who have explicitly opted in to third-party marketing.
* Label the message clearly as a third-party message from Matrix IQ.

{color:#97a0af}*_Optional workaround: non-personalized marketing_*{color}

* You may publish the webinar link as non-targeted, non-personalized content in a neutral in-app placement (e.g. a driver app banner or info center section), without linking it to any user profile.
* This approach avoids the need for consent, provided that:
** The content is visible to all users or a broad, non-individually profiled audience
** No behavioural or profile-based targeting is applied

This is a lower-risk fallback for awareness-building if you cannot confidently segment by consent.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Open questions*
{panel}

* Will Matrix IQ collect personal data (e.g. email, phone) during the webinar registration? If so, are they presenting a GDPR-compliant privacy notice?
* Will we track driver engagement with the link (e.g. click rates, attendance) and share these metrics with Matrix IQ?
* Is this campaign one-off or recurring? If recurring, we may need to treat Matrix IQ as a joint controller depending on collaboration depth / sign a data sharing agreement.

Hi just to add the following email received from Vedovato about the captive fleet test closure.

- Sharing as an FYI
- Sharing to establish the level risk we could actually be exposed to if La Maison du Chauffeur VTC encounters problems DREETS. They comment about potential repercussions on us feels like a slight threat to me.

As a reminder, we never signed a contract with them regarding Captive Fleet. Only an NDA for information sharing.

I’m waiting for them to return from holidays after the 1st September, to meet them and understand what kind of involvement they are hoping for. 


----

Hello Étienne,

Suite à ta demande de mettre fin au programme Captive Fleet, je voulais te faire un retour clair sur les implications côté Serenity Mobilité (et Bolt indirectement), et surtout te proposer une sortie sécurisée et positive pour les chauffeurs.

Les différentes options possibles

Pour mettre fin aux contrats, deux solutions envisagées :

# Licenciement économique collectif, avec plan de sauvegarde de l’emploi (PSE)
# Ruptures conventionnelles individuelles, étalées dans le temps

 

Mais dans les faits, chacune de ces options comporte des contraintes ou des risques

# Plan social :

Mettre en place un plan de sauvegarde de l’emploi (PSE) impliquerait une procédure lourde : notification à la DREETS, plan de reclassement, délais incompressibles, et un encadrement strict — même pour une petite structure comme la nôtre.

Au-delà de la charge administrative, cela pourrait exposer Bolt comme à l’origine d’un plan social, avec les risques d’image et de tensions sociales que cela suppose.

# Faire 15 ruptures conventionnelles rapprochées expose à :

* Blocage potentiel de l’homologation par la DREETS
* Amendes potentielles jusqu’à 35 000 € par salarié en cas d’infraction
* Requalification en licenciement économique collectif déguisé
* Contentieux prud’homaux, si un seul salarié évoque pression ou absence d’alternative

 

Coût estimé par rupture requalifiée → Environ 45 000 €

 

Notre proposition :

Afin d’accélérer, de simplifier et de réduire fortement les risques juridiques, nous proposons 2 solutions de reclassement pour assurer la transition des chauffeurs :

# Intégration dans notre future coopérative VTC

* Statut d’entrepreneur-salarié
* Transfert du contrat de travail avec reprise d’ancienneté 
* Maintien et continuité des avantages sociaux
* Possibilité de conservation du véhicule utilisé actuellement par le chauffeur

 

+Délai de mise en place :+ A réception de notre inscription au Registre VTC (Courant septembre)

 

Cette solution aurait le gros avantage de poursuivre la continuité du contrat de travail et la relation employeur-chauffeur.

 

# Transition vers le statut d’indépendant

* Création d’entreprise et inscription Registre VTC
* Possibilité de conservation du véhicule utilisé actuellement par le chauffeur
* 1 an de suivi comptable + compte bancaire professionnel + accompagnement personnalisé (avec les mêmes interlocuteurs)
* 

 

+Délai de mise en place :+ A réception de leur inscription au Registre VTC (entre 4 et 8 semaines post-création d’entreprise)

 

Pour ceux qui refusent les 2 parcours ci-dessus :

* Rupture conventionnelle ou en dernier ressort, licenciement économique

 

+L’objectif sera d’avoir un minimum de chauffeurs en licenciement économique.+

 

Une implication de Bolt dans cette démarche enverrait un signal fort de continuité et de soutien auprès des chauffeurs pour clôturer positivement ce programme.

Si tu es OK, on peut se caler une réunion pour poser le cadre ensemble et acter les étapes.

À dispo quand tu veux,

 

Bien à toi

 

Nicolas

* Under AXA Insurance contract, we must annually disclose to AXA the *name, DOB* and *country / place of birth* of all French drivers (65k+).
** Purposes are for the contract, litigation, AML, R&D, and personalise services to members. Data will be communicated to AXA Group companies, insurance intermediaries, insurers, partners and authorised professional bodies.
** Current contract does not have any pro-Bolt indemnity.
* Requestor originally asked if we can share these details as well as *home address* and *account creation / deletion date* (based on spreadsheet that requestor was provided).
** Unclear whether this data has always been shared with AXA, due to ownership fog.
* I previously advised:
** We should only share the address if _strictly necessary_. Reporter seems to think it is not, so we should not share for now. Sharing account creation / deletion dates is probably fine, particularly as AXA likely needs this.
** Given the volume of users and need to protect our position, we should enter into a DSA. I prepared one [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ceUCUtJaQmE0ljAAy8b40Bp89EUjLlcO8M8627eanKw/edit?tab=t.0].
*** Data sharing will be both ways (only really in the other direction where a claim is raised directly to AXA - Bolt has right to request claim details, including contact details, medical details, age, gender, race, etc., description of the incident, and of people involved, etc.). I advised that this did not require DSA amendments, as it is sporadic and we are only trying to protect Bolt’s position here.
** I requested some clarity on who else AXA would share the data with. {color:#ff5630}No response on this to date{color}.
* On 8 August, AXA’s team responded with their comments on the DSA (redline is below). 
** No edits to indemnity. Main edits are to the data importer obligations:
*** (i) Removal of requirement to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, in particular those in Annex 2.
**** Given the reputation of AXA, we can probably {color:#36b37e}*accept this*{color} (as it is likely to have decent security measures). Nevertheless, a prudent approach would be: (i) to {color:#ff5630}*flag this risk*{color} to the business (i.e., InfoSec should ideally confirm); and (ii) keep in the general obligation for appropriate security measures (i.e., just remove Annex 2).
*** (ii) Removal of personal data breach notification requirements.
**** We should {color:#ff5630}*push*{color} AXA to explain why they have removed it wholesale. This is an important provision for us. I will include an explanation to sweeten the deal here.
*** (iii) Removal of requirement to promptly deal with DSARs.
**** I am {color:#36b37e}*fine*{color} with this as it is not a deal-breaker. I have aligned it with the suggested text of point (v) below.
*** (iv) Removal of requirement to undertake audits.
**** On balance this is not as important as the other provisions. Given the reputation of the organisation and the importance of the data sharing, IMO{color:#36b37e} *we can allow this*{color}.
*** (iv) Insertion of “_Furthermore, the Parties agree on the principle of good cooperation in the context of exercising data subjects' rights and data breaches. In this regard, they commit to making reasonable efforts to facilitate the exercise of the rights of data subjects and to inform each other in the event of a personal data breach that may concern the insured individuals_”.
**** I am fine with the revised wording re DSRRS. However, we should push back on the data breach notification in the first instance.
** AXA also provided data processing notice, which mentions to Bolt drivers “_As a Bolt partner driver, you automatically benefit from these insurance advantages. By signing, you agree that Bolt may transfer some of your data to AXA in accordance with regulations_” - this is helpful.

** Avoid 1-1 messaging of drivers via WhatsApp off of the back of the channel.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Ops want to ask the following as part of the driver registration flow, so as to understand where drivers are in the process of retrieving their TfL licence. The documents themselves are not be requested - we only want to know where they are in the process:
** (1) DBS completed
** (2) Medical completed
** (3) Topographical assessment completed
** (4) Speaking and listening and SERU assessment completed.
* Ops will then be collecting data on the number of drivers at each stage of the TfL process.
* Ops wants to know whether they can ask these Qs (particularly due to the sensitive nature of medical info).

+*ANALYSIS*+ ([link|https://chatgpt.com/c/68a4e250-49c0-8329-ae57-912e0d2c09fe])

* Items 3 and 4 are very low risk - No concerns from my POV.
** Purpose / legal basis = Operational planning and statistical purposes (“To perform research”) / legitimate interest (arguably covered in our updated privacy notice). No need for LIA, as not high-priority.
* *Sensitive data:* Regarding Items 1 and 2, although it is good that we are not collecting the docs themselves, these still flirt with being {color:#ff5630}*sensitive data*{color}. We want to avoid this, as this will create unnecessary privacy risks.
** *DBS status* - On balance, we should be fine to argue this is not criminal records data, as long as we {color:#4c9aff}*do not ask for the result*{color} (/) 
*** ICO Guidance explains that criminal records data includes data “which is specifically used to learn something about an individual’s criminal record or behaviour”. IMO, simply completing a DBS check, without any indication of the result, tells us nothing about the driver’s criminal record or behaviour.
*** On balance, we can therefore argue that Article 10 is not triggered here. Nevertheless, to be on the safe side, worth exploring mitigations - if we {color:#4c9aff}*immediately aggregate the data upon collection*{color}, this would allow us to sidestep a lot of issues (e.g., legal bases, need for a DPIA). 
** *Medical status* - On balance, we should be fine to argue this is not special category data, as long as we do not ask for the result (/) 
*** Article 4(15) UK GDPR - Data concerning health includes “+*_the provision of health care services_*+_, which reveal information about his or her health status_”.
*** However, ICO guidance shows that in these cases they _“fall under ‘the provision of health care services’ but_ +*_must reveal something about a person’s health status_*+_. For example, a GP or hospital appointment in isolation will not tell you anything about a person’s health as it may be a check-up or screening appointment. However, you could reasonably infer health data from an individual’s list of appointments at an osteopath clinic or from an invoice for a series of physiotherapy sessions”_ ([link|https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/special-category-data/what-is-special-category-data/#scd5]).
*** On balance, we can therefore argue that Article 9 is not triggered here. Nevertheless, to be on the safe side, worth exploring mitigations - if we immediately aggregate the data upon collection, this would allow us to sidestep a lot of issues.
* *Transparency:*{color:#ff5630} *Drivers may also be concerned*{color} about Bolt tracking their application status in this level of detail.
** If drivers feel they are being judged or monitored based on their answers, it could affect willingness to proceed - especially if they aren’t sure how the data will be used.
** As a mitigation, we could {color:#4c9aff}*add a brief explanation*{color} of why this is being collected.
* *Data minimisation*: If the sole goal is pipeline visibility, asking for stage names (e.g. “what step are you on?”) might avoid the sensitivity of yes/no questions on each item. However, this may equally lead to driver’s over-providing info, so on balance the questions are fine as they are (/) 

+*ADVICE*+

* Ultimately, *we should be ok to do this*. But there are some mitigations where we can de-risk this even further.
* Ideally, we should *immediately aggregate the results* as we collect them.
** i.e., Drivers’ answers are not tied to their personal accounts, but only contribute to an aggregated statistics dashboard.
* Ideally, we should also add some *disclaimer text* flagging that this is for insights only and has no effect on onboarding decisions.
** “_To help us understand how drivers are progressing with the Transport for London (TfL) licensing process, please let us know which of the following steps you have already completed. Your answers will only be used for statistical purposes and will not affect your application with Bolt._”

Hello [~accountid:611b95f747d1df00762c6b63], 

I understand your position, which reflects the company’s long-standing view that if our partners do something illegal, we stay passive, as it is not our issue. However, this approach can create serious risks for us as well.

A real-life example: in the LV ride-hailing vertical, some fleets evaded taxes on payments generated via our platform and ended up facing criminal proceedings. As a result, Bolt itself experienced a raid at the office in 2022 (similar incidents happened in Berlin), and one of our former employees in LV still has a criminal case pending. This may be an extreme case, but it illustrates the principle: if a company becomes aware of illegal activities by its partners, fails to implement any controls, due diligence, or procedures to stop them, and continues to benefit from that cooperation, this can be seen as reckless behaviour that may trigger liability for us too.

This is not just a theoretical concern. For example, Estonia’s Commercial Code (§187(1)) requires diligence normally expected of a prudent entrepreneur. At EU level, company law and case law reinforce this *duty of car*e. In particular, CJEU case C-49/16 _Unibet_ establishes that *companies cannot knowingly benefit from unlawful practices of partners without risk of liability.*

Because of this, in the LV ride-hailing vertical we introduced a fleet verification procedure, which includes reviewing public databases to check whether a fleet is paying taxes. If the fleet is classified as high-risk, we suspend it until the records improve.

From this perspective, my advice is to introduce a basic due diligence and KYC process also for Food partners. Doing *at least the minimum* to identify and react to suspicious signs of illegal behaviour (e.g. unpaid taxes, insolvency flags) would align with *the duty of care expected from a prudent operator* and would materially reduce the risk of liability being extended to Bolt if a partner is later found to be non-compliant.

In general we did not find any legal obligation to keep physical documents in the county where the employee is working for most of the countries so except for the few where there is such obligation we don’t see any legal risk storing them in another country, like Estonia, for example. Please be aware that controlling institutions still can requests these documents and we need to provide process how to present them, if requested. For digital document storage there are more local-specific requirements so we need to follow them in each country. 

Please also see GENERAL GUIDELINES - IMPORTANT TO FOLLOW IN ALL COUNTRIES below:

• Digitized documents must be complete, accurate, unalterable, stored securely and accessible to local authorities

• It is safer to keep physical originals of documents that may be necessary later in legal disputes / court (e.g. workplace accidents, tax evidence, fixed-term contracts, termination and settlement agreements, non-compete and confidentiality agreements)

• It’s generally safer to keep wet-ink or notarized documents in physical form

• Maintain detailed records of document conversions, storage, and destruction processes to demonstrate compliance during audits or inspections

• Follow DIN 66399 during destruction (demonstrates compliance during GDPR audit)

• Use certified destruction services and obtain a certificate of destruction

• Use certified services for digitizing, ensuring their legal validity

• Use a qualified electronic signature (QES) in accordance with eIDAS (esp in EU/EEA area)

• Digital records must be easy to print and clearly readable if requested during an audit

• Keep the physical original if a third party (e.g., government agency or court) requires it

• When in doubt, contact legal professionals familiar with the specific country’s labour and data protection laws

The VKI does have the right to demand disclosure of information relevant to their investigations, which could include sharing personal data (though it doesn’t mention it explicitly; but the description of VKI powers is sufficient for us from a GDPR perspective).

From a privacy POV, sharing this data is permissible provided we have a clear process with safeguards in place:

* We only respond to official requests that prove authenticity (not casual emails or WhatsApp messages).
* The VKI must specify exactly whose data they need.

One point to flag: are we confident we can identify the driver in question based on the information the VKI provides? For example, will they give us the driver’s name and surname, and we then return email and address? Prilikom jedne vožnje došlo je do situacije u kojoj je moj kolega ostao s pokvarenim vozilom u blizini moje rute.Kako se radilo o kratkoj udaljenosti i kako nebi ostao na cesti bez pomoči,zamolio sam putnike za dopuštenje da ga usput pokupim.Putnici su se složili i izjavili da im to ne smeta.

Nakon završetka vožnje ,očito je podnesena prijava koja je dovela do mog isključenja. Naglašavam da u niti jednom trenutku nisam imao namjeru prekršiti pravila platforme ili narušiti iskustvo putnika,te mi je žao ako je moj postupak bio shvačen drugačije.

Molim vas da razmotrite okolnosti ovog događaja te da preispitate odluku o mom isključunju. Spreman sam na daljnju suradnju i poštivanje svih pravila platforme kako bih mogao nastaviti raditi putem Bolta.

Ukoliko ipak odlučite ne vratiti moj račun u funkciju ,pozivam se na Uredbu (EU) 2019/1150 o promicanju pravednosti i transparentnosti za poslovanje korisnika internetskih usluga posredovanja,kojom imam pravo na jasno i detaljnoobrazloženje razloga isključenja te dostavom službenog izvješča u pisanom obliku. Molim da mi untom slučaju dostavite takvo izvješče s jasnim navođenjem točnih odredbi pravila koja sam navodno prekršio,kako bih mogao poduzeti daljnje korake.

Ujedno vas obavještavam da cu u slučaju izostanka odgovora ili nedostavljanja traženog izvješca biti prisiljen svoje pravo zaštiti podnošenjem prijave nadležnim tjelima Republike Hrvatske,te ako bude potrebno i pokretanjem postupka pred Europskom komisijom zbog kršenja odredbi navedene uredbe i ograničavanja prava na rad.

Zahvaljujem na razumjevanju i nadam se pozitivnom ishodu.

Srdačan pozdrav! Elvis Đanić

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing to submit an appeal regarding the decision to deactivate my account on the Bolt platform.

During one of my rides, a situation occurred where my colleague’s vehicle broke down near my route. Since it was a short distance away and I did not want to leave him stranded on the road without assistance, I asked my passengers for permission to briefly pick him up on the way. The passengers agreed and stated that they did not mind.

After the ride was completed, it appears that a report was submitted which led to my deactivation. I would like to stress that at no point did I intend to violate the platform’s rules or negatively affect the passengers’ experience, and I regret if my actions were perceived otherwise.

I kindly ask you to take into account the circumstances of this event and to reconsider the decision regarding my deactivation. I am fully willing to continue cooperating and to strictly comply with all platform rules in order to be able to continue working through Bolt.

Should you nevertheless decide not to reinstate my account, I hereby invoke Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services, which grants me the right to receive a clear and detailed explanation of the reasons for deactivation, including a formal written report.

In that case, I kindly request that you provide such a report, clearly stating the exact provisions of the rules I am alleged to have violated, so that I can take further steps if necessary.

I also inform you that, in the event of no response or failure to provide the requested report, I will be forced to protect my rights by submitting a complaint to the competent authorities of the Republic of Croatia and, if necessary, by initiating proceedings before the European Commission due to violations of the provisions of the above-mentioned regulation and restriction of my right to work.

Thank you for your understanding, and I hope for a positive outcome.

Kind regards,
Elvis Đanić
